title: al-ʿAwāmil al-miʾa
author: ʿAbd al-Qāhir al-Jurjānī
subject: nahw
summary: Al-ʿAwāmil al-miʾa, “the hundred governors”, by ʿAbd al-Qāhir al-Jurjānī (d. 471/1078), sets out naḥw as a list of the words and ideas that cause iʿrāb: ninety-one heard governors in thirteen kinds, seven analogical ones and two abstract ones. On the Indian path it is read after Naḥw-i Mīr, often with its commentary, the Sharḥ Miʾat ʿāmil; the Ottoman madrasas read it too, and Birgivī wrote his “new” ʿAwāmil after it. Each kind is named by what it does, counted, listed and shown in short examples, so that the student learns by heart a map of what governs what. The lessons follow the vowelled text printed by A. Lockett (Calcutta, 1814) a kind at a time, and explain each governor on the book's own examples.

lessons.title: A hundred governors and their divisions
body: After the basmala and the name of its author, the book gives a count: the governors (ʿawāmil) of naḥw are a hundred. A governor (ʿāmil) is whatever causes the ending of another word: the particle bi- that puts Zayd in jarr in marartu bi-Zaydin, “I passed by Zayd”, or the verb kāna that puts qāʾiman in naṣb in kāna Zaydun qāʾiman, “Zayd was standing”. The book does not define the governor; it lists the governors, so that the student who knows the list can name the cause of the endings he reads.

The first division is into expressed (lafẓiyya) and abstract (maʿnawiyya). An expressed governor is a word you can hear and point to, such as bi- or kāna. An abstract governor is not a word at all but a state of the sentence, such as a noun's standing at its head with nothing before it. Of the hundred, ninety-eight are expressed and two are abstract.

The expressed governors are again of two kinds. The heard ones (samāʿiyya) are ninety-one words whose working is known only from the usage of the Arabs: nothing but their speech tells us that rubba puts its noun in jarr or that lan puts the verb in naṣb, so these are learnt one by one, as a list. The analogical ones (qiyāsiyya) are seven classes of word governed by a rule, such as “the verb governs”: any word of the class governs in the same way without being listed. So 91 + 7 + 2 = 100.

The ninety-one heard governors fall into thirteen kinds, which the book takes in turn: six kinds of particles, three of nouns and four of verbs. Each kind is named by what it does (“particles that put only the noun in jarr”, “particles that put the noun in naṣb and the predicate in rafʿ”), then counted, listed and shown in short examples. The student learns the list by heart and then reads it with a commentary; Lockett's print, which our text follows, has the Arabic Sharḥ Miʾat ʿāmil after it.

Two cautions. “Heard” does not mean rare: the particles of jarr and inna are among the commonest words of the language; it means only that their working is learnt from usage, not worked out by a rule. And the count is a way of teaching: Birgivī, who knew this book, counted sixty governors in his al-ʿAwāmil al-jadīda, dividing much the same material another way.

tasks.prompt: Add up the hundred governors by their divisions, and the heard ones by their three groups.
tasks.answer: Heard 91 + analogical 7 + abstract 2 = 100. The heard ones are 41 particles (kinds 1–6: 17 + 6 + 2 + 7 + 4 + 5), 22 nouns (kinds 7–9: 9 + 4 + 9) and 28 verbs (kinds 10–13: 13 + 4 + 4 + 7).

tasks.prompt: Is each governor expressed or abstract, and if expressed, heard or analogical? (a) bi- in marartu bi-Zaydin; (b) kāna in kāna Zaydun qāʾiman; (c) what puts Zaydun in rafʿ in Zaydun fī al-dāri, “Zayd is in the house”.
tasks.arabic: مَرَرْتُ بِزَيْدٍ — كَانَ زَيْدٌ قَائِمًا — زَيْدٌ فِي الدَّارِ
tasks.answer: (a) Expressed and heard: a particle of jarr, the first kind. (b) Expressed and heard: an incomplete verb, the tenth kind. (c) Abstract: no word stands before Zaydun; its standing at the head of the sentence (the ibtidāʾ) puts it in rafʿ.

tasks.prompt: Why must the heard governors be learnt as a list, while the analogical ones need not be?
tasks.answer: The working of a heard governor is known only from the usage of the Arabs: no rule tells us that rubba gives jarr or lan gives naṣb, so each word is learnt by itself. An analogical governor is a class with a rule, such as “the verb governs”, so every word of the class governs without being named.

quiz.prompt: How many governors does al-Jurjānī count?
quiz.explanation: Ninety-one heard, seven analogical and two abstract: a hundred.

quiz.prompt: Why is a governor called “heard”?

quiz.prompt: Which is an analogical governor?
quiz.explanation: The verb governs by a rule that covers every verb; rubba, lan and inna are heard governors.

quiz.explanation: In marartu bi-Zaydin, bi- is the governor of Zaydin: it causes its jarr.

text.original: بِسْمِ اللَّهِ الرَّحْمَنِ الرَّحِيمِ. الْعَوَامِلُ فِي النَّحْوِ عَلَى مَا أَلَّفَهُ الشَّيْخُ الْإِمَامُ الْفَاضِلُ عَبْدُ الْقَاهِرِ بْنُ عَبْدِ الرَّحْمَنِ الْجُرْجَانِيُّ، سَقَى اللَّهُ ثَرَاهُ وَجَعَلَ الْجَنَّةَ مَثْوَاهُ، مِائَةُ عَامِلٍ: مِنْهَا لَفْظِيَّةٌ، وَمِنْهَا مَعْنَوِيَّةٌ. فَاللَّفْظِيَّةُ مِنْهَا عَلَى ضَرْبَيْنِ: سَمَاعِيَّةٌ وَقِيَاسِيَّةٌ. فَالسَّمَاعِيَّةُ مِنْهَا أَحَدٌ وَتِسْعُونَ عَامِلًا، وَالْقِيَاسِيَّةُ مِنْهَا سَبْعَةُ عَوَامِلَ، وَالْمَعْنَوِيَّةُ مِنْهَا عَدَدَانِ. فَالسَّمَاعِيَّةُ تَتَنَوَّعُ عَلَى ثَلَاثَةَ عَشَرَ نَوْعًا.
text.en: In the name of God, the Merciful, the Compassionate. The governors (al-ʿawāmil) in grammar, according to what the Shaykh, the Imam, the learned ʿAbd al-Qāhir ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Jurjānī composed (may God water the earth of his grave and make Paradise his abode), are a hundred governors. Some of them are expressed (lafẓiyya) and some abstract (maʿnawiyya). The expressed ones are of two kinds: heard (samāʿiyya) and analogical (qiyāsiyya). The heard ones are ninety-one governors, the analogical ones seven governors, and the abstract ones two in number. The heard ones are divided into thirteen kinds.

lessons.title: The first kind: the seventeen particles of jarr
body: The first kind is the particles that “put only the noun in jarr”: seventeen particles, each governing the one noun after it, which takes the kasra or another sign of jarr. “Only” (faqaṭ) sets this kind apart from the next: a particle of jarr governs one word and nothing more, while inna and its sisters govern two, a noun and a predicate. And it governs nouns alone: jarr belongs to the noun and never to the verb. The particle is called jārr, the noun after it majrūr, and the two together a jārr wa-majrūr.

Most of them are everyday words with plain meanings, and the book's examples show them: marartu bi-Zaydin, “I passed by Zayd”; sirtu mina al-baṣrati ilā al-kūfati, “I travelled from Basra to Kufa”, min for the starting point and ilā for the end; ramaytu al-sahma ʿani al-qawsi, “I shot the arrow from the bow”, ʿan for moving away; Zaydun fī al-dāri, “Zayd is in the house”; al-mālu li-Zaydin, “the money is Zayd's”, li- for belonging; Zaydun ʿalā al-saṭḥi, “on the roof”; Zaydun ka-al-asadi, “like the lion”. Five of them are a single letter joined to the noun: bi-, li-, ka-, and the wāw and the tāʾ of the oath.

Some need a word more. Rubba, “many a”, comes only before an indefinite noun (rajulin, never al-rajuli), and in the book's example a sentence describes that noun: rubba rajulin laqītuhu, “many a man have I met”. Mudh and mundhu, “since”, come before a time: mā raʾaytuhu mundhu yawmi al-jumuʿati, “I have not seen him since Friday”. Ḥattā, “up to”, marks the end of a thing: akaltu al-samakata ḥattā raʾsihā, “I ate the fish up to its head”. The grammarians know this sentence with three endings: raʾsihā, as here, with ḥattā a particle of jarr; raʾsahā, with ḥattā joining the head to the fish, “I ate the fish, even its head”; and raʾsuhā, a new sentence, “even its head [was eaten]”. The book gives the first, because this is the chapter of jarr.

The wāw and the tāʾ of the oath put in jarr the name sworn by: wa-Allāhi and ta-Allāhi, “by God”. What is sworn to follows as a sentence of its own: la-afʿalanna kadhā, “I shall surely do such-and-such”. The wāw swears by any name; the tāʾ is used almost only with the name of God.

The last three, ḥāshā, khalā and ʿadā, mean “except”: they take one noun out of the rest, jāʾanī al-qawmu ḥāshā Zaydin, “the people came to me, except Zayd”. The book counts them as particles of jarr, and so they are when the noun after them is in jarr. The grammarians also use khalā and ʿadā, and some ḥāshā too, as verbs, with the noun after them in naṣb; that belongs to the chapter of exception, and the fourth kind will give illā, which puts the excepted noun in naṣb.

A trap: in marartu bi-Zaydin the governor of Zaydin is bi-, not the verb marartu. The verb reaches Zayd only through the particle, and the jarr is the particle's work. Whenever a noun follows one of the seventeen, ask first whether the particle is its governor.

tasks.answer: ʿAn governs al-qawsi; li- governs Zaydin; ʿalā governs al-saṭḥi. Each noun is in jarr, shown by the kasra. (The kasra on ʿani is only a vowel to join it to the next word.)

tasks.prompt: Why does the book say rubba rajulin, and why would rubba al-rajuli be wrong?
tasks.answer: Rubba comes only before an indefinite noun: rajulin, “a man”, not al-rajuli, “the man”. It speaks of many men of a kind, not of one known man.

tasks.prompt: Give the three readings of akaltu al-samakata ḥattā raʾs-, and say which belongs to this chapter.
tasks.answer: Raʾsihā, in jarr: ḥattā is a particle of jarr, “up to its head”; this is the book's reading and this chapter's. Raʾsahā, in naṣb: ḥattā joins the head to al-samakata, “even its head”. Raʾsuhā, in rafʿ: a new sentence, “even its head [was eaten]”.

tasks.prompt: In marartu bi-Zaydin, what is the governor of Zaydin: the verb or the particle?
tasks.answer: The particle bi-. The verb marartu reaches Zayd only through it, and the jarr of Zaydin is the particle's work.

quiz.prompt: How many particles of jarr does this book count?
quiz.explanation: Seventeen, from the bāʾ to ʿadā; Birgivī's al-ʿAwāmil al-jadīda counts twenty.

quiz.prompt: What does “only” (faqaṭ) say about this kind?
options: They are used only in verse
Each particle governs one noun and nothing more
quiz.explanation: A particle of jarr governs the single noun after it; the next kind governs a noun and a predicate.

quiz.prompt: Rubba comes only before…
quiz.explanation: Rubba rajulin, “many a man”: never rubba al-rajuli.

quiz.prompt: In mā raʾaytuhu mundhu yawmi al-jumuʿati, mundhu means…
quiz.explanation: Mudh and mundhu come before a time: “I have not seen him since Friday”.

quiz.prompt: Which particle is used in an oath?
quiz.explanation: The wāw and the tāʾ of the oath: wa-Allāhi, ta-Allāhi, “by God”.

quiz.prompt: In jāʾanī al-qawmu ḥāshā Zaydin, Zaydin is…
quiz.explanation: The book counts ḥāshā among the particles of jarr: the excepted noun is in jarr.

quiz.prompt: In al-mālu li-Zaydin, the lām means…
quiz.explanation: “The money is Zayd's”: the lām of belonging.

text.original: النَّوْعُ الْأَوَّلُ: حُرُوفٌ تَجُرُّ الِاسْمَ فَقَطْ، وَهِيَ سَبْعَةَ عَشَرَ حَرْفًا: الْبَاءُ، وَمِنْ، وَعَنْ، وَإِلَى، وَفِي، وَاللَّامُ، وَرُبَّ، وَعَلَى، وَالْكَافُ، وَمُذْ، وَمُنْذُ، وَحَتَّى، وَوَاوُ الْقَسَمِ وَتَاؤُهُ، وَحَاشَا، وَخَلَا، وَعَدَا.
text.en: The first kind: particles that put only the noun in jarr. They are seventeen particles: the bāʾ (bi-), min “from”, ʿan “away from”, ilā “to”, fī “in”, the lām (li-), rubba “many a”, ʿalā “on”, the kāf (ka-) “like”, mudh and mundhu “since”, ḥattā “up to”, the wāw and the tāʾ of the oath, ḥāshā, khalā and ʿadā “except”.

text.original: نَحْوُ: مَرَرْتُ بِزَيْدٍ، وَسِرْتُ مِنَ الْبَصْرَةِ إِلَى الْكُوفَةِ، وَرَمَيْتُ السَّهْمَ عَنِ الْقَوْسِ، وَزَيْدٌ فِي الدَّارِ، وَالْمَالُ لِزَيْدٍ، وَرُبَّ رَجُلٍ لَقِيتُهُ، وَزَيْدٌ عَلَى السَّطْحِ، وَزَيْدٌ كَالْأَسَدِ، وَمَا رَأَيْتُهُ مُذْ وَمُنْذُ يَوْمِ الْجُمُعَةِ، وَأَكَلْتُ السَّمَكَةَ حَتَّى رَأْسِهَا، وَوَاللَّهِ لَأَفْعَلَنَّ كَذَا، وَتَاللَّهِ لَأَفْعَلَنَّ كَذَا، وَجَاءَنِي الْقَوْمُ حَاشَا زَيْدٍ، وَرَأَيْتُ الْقَوْمَ خَلَا زَيْدٍ، وَمَرَرْتُ بِالْقَوْمِ عَدَا زَيْدٍ.
text.en: As marartu bi-Zaydin “I passed by Zayd”, sirtu mina al-baṣrati ilā al-kūfati “I travelled from Basra to Kufa”, ramaytu al-sahma ʿani al-qawsi “I shot the arrow from the bow”, Zaydun fī al-dāri “Zayd is in the house”, al-mālu li-Zaydin “the money belongs to Zayd”, rubba rajulin laqītuhu “many a man have I met”, Zaydun ʿalā al-saṭḥi “Zayd is on the roof”, Zaydun ka-al-asadi “Zayd is like the lion”, mā raʾaytuhu mudh and mundhu yawmi al-jumuʿati “I have not seen him since Friday”, akaltu al-samakata ḥattā raʾsihā “I ate the fish up to its head”, wa-Allāhi la-afʿalanna kadhā and ta-Allāhi la-afʿalanna kadhā “by God, I shall surely do such-and-such”, jāʾanī al-qawmu ḥāshā Zaydin “the people came to me, except Zayd”, raʾaytu al-qawma khalā Zaydin “I saw the people, except Zayd” and marartu bi-al-qawmi ʿadā Zaydin “I passed by the people, except Zayd”.

lessons.title: Inna and its sisters; mā and lā like laysa
lessons.arabic: إِنَّ وَأَخَوَاتُهَا، وَمَا وَلَا الْمُشَبَّهَتَانِ بِلَيْسَ
lessons.transliteration: inna wa-akhawātuhā, wa-mā wa-lā al-mushabbahatān bi-laysa
body: The second kind governs two words at once, a noun and its predicate (khabar): six particles that “put the noun in naṣb and the predicate in rafʿ”. They come before a sentence of subject and predicate and change its first ending: Zaydun qāʾimun, “Zayd is standing”, becomes inna Zaydan qāʾimun, “Zayd is indeed standing”. The first word, now in naṣb, is called the noun (ism) of inna; the second stays in rafʿ as its predicate (khabar).

Each brings its own meaning. Inna, “indeed”, confirms the sentence. Anna, “that”, makes the whole sentence a part of another one: in balaghanī anna Zaydan munṭaliqun, “it has reached me that Zayd is setting off”, anna with its noun and predicate stands for a maṣdar, “Zayd's setting off”, and is the doer of balagha. Kaʾanna, “as if”, likens: kaʾanna Zaydan asadun. Lākinna, “but”, corrects what came before: qāma Zaydun lākinna ʿAmran jālisun, “Zayd stood up, but ʿAmr is sitting”. Layta, “if only”, wishes, even for what cannot be: layta al-shabāba ʿāʾidun, “if only youth were coming back”. Laʿalla, “perhaps”, hopes: laʿalla ʿAmran khārijun.

The madrasa calls them “the particles that resemble the verb” (al-ḥurūf al-mushabbaha bi-l-fiʿl). The commentators give the reasons: like a past verb they have three letters or more and end in a fatḥa; they carry a verb's meaning (inna is “I confirm”, layta “I wish”); and they govern two words, one in rafʿ and one in naṣb, like a verb whose object has been put before its doer.

The third kind is the mirror image of the second: two particles that “put the noun in rafʿ and the predicate in naṣb”, mā and lā, “which resemble laysa”, “is not”. Laysa, one of the incomplete verbs of the tenth kind, gives rafʿ to its noun and naṣb to its predicate; mā and lā, which also negate, borrow its work: mā Zaydun fāḍilan, “Zayd is not excellent”; lā rajulun afḍala minka, “no man is better than you”. This is the usage of the people of the Ḥijāz, in which the Qurʾān says mā hādhā basharan (Q 12:31); the Banū Tamīm leave mā without work and say mā Zaydun fāḍilun.

Two traps. The lā of this kind takes indefinite nouns and leaves them with tanwīn, rajulun; it is not the lā that denies a whole genus, lā rajula fī al-dāri, “there is no man in the house”, which takes a fatḥa without tanwīn and works like inna. And do not confuse the two mirror kinds: with inna the first noun is in naṣb (inna Zaydan qāʾimun), with mā the second (mā Zaydun fāḍilan).

tasks.prompt: Give the iʿrāb of kaʾanna Zaydan asadun.
tasks.answer: Kaʾanna: a particle that resembles the verb, of likening. Zaydan: its noun, in naṣb by the fatḥa. Asadun: its predicate, in rafʿ by the ḍamma. “It is as if Zayd were a lion.”

tasks.prompt: Why is the predicate fāḍilan in mā Zaydun fāḍilan, but fāḍilun in Zaydun fāḍilun?
tasks.answer: Mā here resembles laysa and works like it: its noun Zaydun stays in rafʿ and its predicate is put in naṣb. Without mā, both subject and predicate are in rafʿ. (The Banū Tamīm, who do not let mā work, would say mā Zaydun fāḍilun.)

tasks.prompt: In balaghanī anna Zaydan munṭaliqun, what is the doer of balagha?
tasks.answer: Anna with its noun and predicate, taken together as a maṣdar: “Zayd's setting off has reached me”. The -nī is the object of balagha.

tasks.prompt: Name the noun and the predicate, with their states, in layta al-shabāba ʿāʾidun and lā rajulun afḍala minka.
tasks.arabic: لَيْتَ الشَّبَابَ عَائِدٌ — لَا رَجُلٌ أَفْضَلَ مِنْكَ
tasks.answer: Layta: al-shabāba is its noun, in naṣb; ʿāʾidun its predicate, in rafʿ. Lā (like laysa): rajulun is its noun, in rafʿ; afḍala its predicate, in naṣb (afḍal takes no tanwīn), with minka after it.

quiz.prompt: Inna and its sisters put…
options: the noun in rafʿ and the predicate in naṣb
the noun in naṣb and the predicate in rafʿ
quiz.explanation: Inna Zaydan qāʾimun: the noun Zaydan in naṣb, the predicate qāʾimun in rafʿ.

quiz.prompt: How many particles are in the second kind?
quiz.explanation: Inna, anna, kaʾanna, lākinna, layta and laʿalla.

quiz.prompt: Which particle expresses a wish?
quiz.explanation: Layta al-shabāba ʿāʾidun, “if only youth were coming back”: a wish, even for what cannot be.

quiz.prompt: The mā and lā of the third kind resemble…
quiz.explanation: Like laysa, they negate and give rafʿ to the noun and naṣb to the predicate.

quiz.prompt: In mā Zaydun fāḍilan, fāḍilan is…
options: the noun of mā, in naṣb
the predicate of mā, in naṣb
quiz.explanation: Zaydun is the noun of mā in rafʿ, fāḍilan its predicate in naṣb.

quiz.prompt: Kaʾanna Zaydan asadun means…
options: it is as if Zayd were a lion
quiz.explanation: Kaʾanna is the particle of likening.

quiz.prompt: In lā rajulun afḍala minka, rajulun is…
options: the predicate of lā, in rafʿ
the noun of lā, in rafʿ
quiz.explanation: The lā that resembles laysa gives rafʿ to its noun and naṣb to its predicate, afḍala.

text.original: النَّوْعُ الثَّانِي: حُرُوفٌ تَنْصِبُ الِاسْمَ وَتَرْفَعُ الْخَبَرَ، وَهِيَ سِتَّةُ أَحْرُفٍ: إِنَّ، وَأَنَّ، وَكَأَنَّ، وَلَكِنَّ، وَلَيْتَ، وَلَعَلَّ، نَحْوُ: إِنَّ زَيْدًا قَائِمٌ، وَبَلَغَنِي أَنَّ زَيْدًا مُنْطَلِقٌ، وَكَأَنَّ زَيْدًا أَسَدٌ، وَقَامَ زَيْدٌ لَكِنَّ عَمْرًا جَالِسٌ، وَلَيْتَ الشَّبَابَ عَائِدٌ، وَلَعَلَّ عَمْرًا خَارِجٌ.
text.en: The second kind: particles that put the noun in naṣb and the predicate in rafʿ. They are six particles: inna, anna, kaʾanna, lākinna, layta and laʿalla, as inna Zaydan qāʾimun “Zayd is indeed standing”, balaghanī anna Zaydan munṭaliqun “it has reached me that Zayd is setting off”, kaʾanna Zaydan asadun “it is as if Zayd were a lion”, qāma Zaydun lākinna ʿAmran jālisun “Zayd stood up, but ʿAmr is sitting”, layta al-shabāba ʿāʾidun “if only youth were coming back” and laʿalla ʿAmran khārijun “perhaps ʿAmr is going out”.

text.original: النَّوْعُ الثَّالِثُ: حَرْفَانِ تَرْفَعَانِ الِاسْمَ وَتَنْصِبَانِ الْخَبَرَ، وَهُمَا مَا وَلَا الْمُشَبَّهَتَانِ بِلَيْسَ، نَحْوُ: مَا زَيْدٌ فَاضِلًا، وَلَا رَجُلٌ أَفْضَلَ مِنْكَ.
text.en: The third kind: two particles that put the noun in rafʿ and the predicate in naṣb. They are mā and lā, which resemble laysa, as mā Zaydun fāḍilan “Zayd is not excellent” and lā rajulun afḍala minka “no man is better than you”.

lessons.title: The fourth kind: particles that put only the noun in naṣb
body: The fourth kind is seven particles that put one noun in naṣb and do nothing more: the wāw, illā, and five particles of calling (nidāʾ), yā, ayā, hayā, ay and the hamza with fatḥa. Like the particles of jarr, each governs a single noun; but where those gave jarr, these give naṣb.

The wāw here is not the wāw of “and”, which joins a word to the one before it in the same state, nor the wāw of the oath. It is the wāw of accompaniment (al-maʿiyya), meaning “with”: istawā al-māʾu wa-al-khashabata, “the water rose level with the plank”. The water and the plank did not both rise: the water rose until it stood level with the plank, so the plank cannot share the verb with the water, and it is put in naṣb. The grammarians call it the object of accompaniment (al-mafʿūl maʿahu). Many of them say that the verb governs it, through the wāw; al-Jurjānī counts the wāw itself as its governor.

Illā, “except”, takes one out of a group: jāʾanī al-qawmu illā Zaydan, “the people came to me except Zayd”. Zayd is the excepted (al-mustathnā), in naṣb; the people are what he is taken out of (al-mustathnā minhu). Compare ḥāshā Zaydin in the first kind: the same meaning, but there the noun was in jarr. The naṣb is the rule when the sentence is positive and complete, as here; in a negative sentence (mā jāʾanī aḥadun illā Zaydun) another ending is allowed, which later books teach.

The five particles of calling put the one called (al-munādā) in naṣb when he is named by the first term of an iḍāfa, as ʿAbd Allāh: yā ʿAbda Allāhi, “O ʿAbd Allāh”. The book gives the same name with all five: ayā ʿAbda Allāhi, hayā ʿAbda Allāhi, ay ʿAbda Allāhi, a-ʿAbda Allāhi. The commentators add that ayā and hayā are for calling one who is far, the hamza and ay for one who is near, and yā for either.

A trap: the one called is not always in naṣb. A single name called by itself takes a ḍamma without tanwīn: yā Zaydu, “O Zayd!”; that ending is fixed (mabnī), not a sign of rafʿ. The book chose ʿAbd Allāh, a muḍāf, because there the naṣb shows.

the excepted noun, after illā
the one called
the particles of calling: yā, ayā, hayā, ay, a-

tasks.arabic: جَاءَنِي الْقَوْمُ إِلَّا زَيْدًا — اسْتَوَى الْمَاءُ وَالْخَشَبَةَ — هَيَا عَبْدَ اللَّهِ
tasks.answer: Illā governs Zaydan, the excepted. The wāw of accompaniment governs al-khashabata (in al-Jurjānī's count). Hayā, a particle of calling, governs ʿAbda, the one called; Allāhi is in jarr by iḍāfa.

tasks.prompt: Why is al-khashabata in naṣb, and not in rafʿ like al-māʾu?
tasks.answer: The wāw does not join the plank to the water as a second doer: only the water rose. It means “with”, and the noun after it is the mafʿūl maʿahu, in naṣb.

tasks.prompt: Compare jāʾanī al-qawmu illā Zaydan with jāʾanī al-qawmu ḥāshā Zaydin. What is the same, and what differs?
tasks.arabic: جَاءَنِي الْقَوْمُ إِلَّا زَيْدًا — جَاءَنِي الْقَوْمُ حَاشَا زَيْدٍ
tasks.answer: The meaning is the same: Zayd is taken out of the people who came. The ending differs: illā puts the excepted in naṣb (fourth kind), ḥāshā as a particle of jarr puts it in jarr (first kind).

tasks.prompt: Why does the book call “O ʿAbd Allāh” and not “O Zayd” to show the naṣb?
tasks.answer: A single name called by itself is fixed on the ḍamma: yā Zaydu. The one called shows naṣb when he is named by a muḍāf, as ʿAbda Allāhi.

quiz.prompt: How many particles are in the fourth kind?
quiz.explanation: The wāw, illā, and the five particles of calling.

quiz.prompt: The wāw in istawā al-māʾu wa-al-khashabata means…
quiz.explanation: The wāw of accompaniment: the water rose level with the plank.

quiz.prompt: In jāʾanī al-qawmu illā Zaydan, Zaydan is…
quiz.explanation: Illā takes Zayd out of the people; he is the mustathnā, in naṣb.

quiz.prompt: Which is NOT a particle of calling?
quiz.explanation: Illā is the particle of exception; yā, ayā, hayā, ay and the hamza call.

quiz.prompt: In yā ʿAbda Allāhi, ʿAbda is in naṣb because…
options: it is called and is the first term of an iḍāfa
it is the object of a verb
yā is a particle of jarr
quiz.explanation: The one called is in naṣb when he is a muḍāf, as ʿAbd Allāh.

quiz.prompt: How is Zayd called by his name alone?
quiz.explanation: A single name is fixed on the ḍamma without tanwīn.

quiz.prompt: According to the commentators, hayā is used to call…
quiz.explanation: Ayā and hayā for the far, the hamza and ay for the near, yā for either.

text.original: النَّوْعُ الرَّابِعُ: حُرُوفٌ تَنْصِبُ الِاسْمَ فَقَطْ، وَهِيَ سَبْعَةُ أَحْرُفٍ: الْوَاوُ، وَإِلَّا، وَيَا، وَأَيَا، وَهَيَا، وَأَيْ، وَالْهَمْزَةُ الْمَفْتُوحَةُ، نَحْوُ: اسْتَوَى الْمَاءُ وَالْخَشَبَةَ، وَجَاءَنِي الْقَوْمُ إِلَّا زَيْدًا، وَيَا عَبْدَ اللَّهِ، وَأَيَا عَبْدَ اللَّهِ، وَهَيَا عَبْدَ اللَّهِ، وَأَيْ عَبْدَ اللَّهِ، وَأَعَبْدَ اللَّهِ.
text.en: The fourth kind: particles that put only the noun in naṣb. They are seven particles: the wāw, illā, yā, ayā, hayā, ay and the hamza with fatḥa, as istawā al-māʾu wa-al-khashabata “the water rose level with the plank”, jāʾanī al-qawmu illā Zaydan “the people came to me except Zayd”, yā ʿAbda Allāhi “O ʿAbd Allāh”, ayā ʿAbda Allāhi, hayā ʿAbda Allāhi, ay ʿAbda Allāhi and a-ʿAbda Allāhi.

lessons.title: The fifth kind: particles that put the muḍāriʿ in naṣb
body: With the fifth kind the governors turn from the noun to the verb. Of the verbs only the muḍāriʿ, the present-future verb, takes iʿrāb: it is in rafʿ when nothing governs it (taḍribu, “you hit”), and four particles put it in naṣb: an, lan, kay and idhan. The sign of naṣb is the fatḥa on the last letter, taḍribu → an taḍriba, or, in the forms that end in a nūn, the dropping of that nūn: taḍribāni → lan taḍribā.

An, “that”, gives the verb the sense of a maṣdar: karihtu an taḍriba, “I disliked that you should hit”, is “I disliked your hitting”. An with its verb fills the place of a noun, here the object of karihtu; for this the grammarians call it al-maṣdariyya. Naḥw-i Mīr, read before this book, explains it the same way: urīdu an taqūma, “I want you to stand”, is urīdu qiyāmaka, “I want your standing”.

Lan negates the future: lan tafʿala, “you will not do it”. Kay gives the purpose, “so that”: jiʾtuka kay tuʿṭiyanī ḥaqqī, “I came to you so that you would give me my due”. There the naṣb shows as a fatḥa on the yāʾ of tuʿṭiya, before the pronoun -nī.

Idhan, “then, in that case”, begins an answer to what another has said: to a man who says aslamtu, “I have become a Muslim”, you reply idhan tadkhula al-jannata, “then you will enter Paradise”. The book's words “in answer to” are the key: idhan stands at the head of an answer, and the verb after it speaks of the future. Later books add that nothing may come between idhan and its verb but an oath or the lā of negation.

Do not confuse lan with lam. Lan yaḍriba, “he will not hit”, puts the verb in naṣb and speaks of the future; lam yaḍrib, “he did not hit”, which the next lesson gives, puts it in jazm and speaks of the past. One letter and one vowel tell them apart.

the an that gives its verb the sense of a maṣdar
“will not”: negation of the future
“then, in that case”: at the head of an answer

tasks.answer: Lan taḍriba: the fatḥa. Lan taḍribā and lan taḍribū: the nūn is dropped.

tasks.prompt: What does an do in karihtu an taḍriba? Say the sentence again in English with a maṣdar.
tasks.answer: An puts taḍriba in naṣb and gives it the sense of a maṣdar; an with its verb is the object of karihtu: “I disliked your hitting”.

tasks.prompt: Someone says aslamtu, “I have become a Muslim”. Answer him with idhan as the book does, and say why the verb is in naṣb.
tasks.answer: Idhan tadkhula al-jannata, “then you will enter Paradise”. Idhan stands at the head of the answer, the verb speaks of the future and nothing comes between them, so idhan puts tadkhula in naṣb.

tasks.prompt: Lan yaḍriba and lam yaḍrib: which is in naṣb, and of what time does each speak?
tasks.answer: Lan yaḍriba is in naṣb (the fatḥa) and negates the future, “he will not hit”. Lam yaḍrib is in jazm (the sukūn) and negates the past, “he did not hit”.

quiz.explanation: Tuʿṭī becomes tuʿṭiya: the fatḥa shows on its last letter, the yāʾ.

text.original: النَّوْعُ الْخَامِسُ: حُرُوفٌ تَنْصِبُ الْفِعْلَ الْمُضَارِعَ، وَهِيَ أَرْبَعَةُ أَحْرُفٍ: أَنْ، وَلَنْ، وَكَيْ، وَإِذَنْ، نَحْوُ: كَرِهْتُ أَنْ تَضْرِبَ، وَلَنْ تَفْعَلَ، وَجِئْتُكَ كَيْ تُعْطِيَنِي حَقِّي، وَإِذَنْ تَدْخُلَ الْجَنَّةَ فِي جَوَابِ: أَسْلَمْتُ.
text.en: The fifth kind: particles that put the muḍāriʿ in naṣb. They are four particles: an, lan, kay and idhan, as karihtu an taḍriba “I disliked that you should hit”, lan tafʿala “you will not do [it]”, jiʾtuka kay tuʿṭiyanī ḥaqqī “I came to you so that you would give me my due”, and idhan tadkhula al-jannata “then you will enter Paradise”, in answer to aslamtu “I have become a Muslim”.

lessons.title: The sixth kind: particles that put the muḍāriʿ in jazm
body: Five particles put the muḍāriʿ in jazm: in, lam, lammā, the lām of command and the lā of prohibition. Jazm belongs to the verb alone, as jarr belongs to the noun. Its sign is the sukūn on the last letter, yaḍribu → lam yaḍrib, or, in the forms that end in a nūn, the dropping of that nūn: yaḍribāni → lam yaḍribā, yaḍribūna → lam yaḍribū. (A verb that ends in a weak letter loses that letter instead; that is taught in ṣarf.)

In, “if”, the particle of condition, governs two verbs: the condition (al-sharṭ) and its answer (al-jazāʾ): in tukrimnī ukrimka, “if you honour me, I shall honour you”. Both tukrim and ukrim are in jazm; the -nī and the -ka are object pronouns joined to them. Because in governs two verbs with the meaning “if”, it is the model of the next kind: nine nouns that put the verb in jazm “in the meaning of in”.

Lam and lammā both negate the past while governing a muḍāriʿ: lam yaḍrib Zaydun, “Zayd did not hit”; lammā yaḍrib Zaydun, “Zayd has not yet hit”. Lam turns the present form to a past meaning; lammā adds that the negation lasts up to now and that the hitting is still expected.

The lām of command, li-, gives an order to one who is absent: li-yaḍrib Zaydun, “let Zayd hit”. The lā of prohibition forbids: lā taḍrib Zaydan, “do not hit Zayd”. The print names it lāʾ al-nahy, speaking of the particle lā as a noun.

A trap: lā before a muḍāriʿ is not always prohibition. Lā taḍribu, with the ḍamma, only negates, “you do not hit”, and leaves the verb in rafʿ; lā taḍrib, with the sukūn, forbids, “do not hit!”. The vowel of the last letter tells you which lā you are reading.

the condition and its answer
“not yet”: negation of the past lasting up to now
the lām of command, to one absent
the lā of prohibition

tasks.prompt: In in tukrimnī ukrimka, name the governor, the two verbs it governs and their state.
tasks.answer: The governor is in, the particle of condition. It governs tukrim, the condition, and ukrim, the answer; both are in jazm, shown by the sukūn.

tasks.prompt: What is the difference in meaning between lam yaḍrib Zaydun and lammā yaḍrib Zaydun?

tasks.answer: Both deny the hitting in the past. Lam says only that it did not happen; lammā says that it has not happened up to now and is still expected: “not yet”.

tasks.answer: Lā taḍribu: the lā of negation, the verb in rafʿ, “you do not hit”. Lā taḍrib: the lā of prohibition, the verb in jazm, “do not hit!”.

quiz.explanation: In governs the condition and its answer.

text.original: النَّوْعُ السَّادِسُ: حُرُوفٌ تَجْزِمُ الْفِعْلَ الْمُضَارِعَ، وَهِيَ خَمْسَةُ أَحْرُفٍ: إِنْ، وَلَمْ، وَلَمَّا، وَلَامُ الْأَمْرِ، وَلَاءُ النَّهْيِ، نَحْوُ: إِنْ تُكْرِمْنِي أُكْرِمْكَ، وَلَمْ يَضْرِبْ زَيْدٌ، وَلَمَّا يَضْرِبْ زَيْدٌ، وَلِيَضْرِبْ زَيْدٌ، وَلَا تَضْرِبْ زَيْدًا.
text.en: The sixth kind: particles that put the muḍāriʿ in jazm. They are five particles: in, lam, lammā, the lām of command and the lā of prohibition, as in tukrimnī ukrimka “if you honour me, I shall honour you”, lam yaḍrib Zaydun “Zayd did not hit”, lammā yaḍrib Zaydun “Zayd has not yet hit”, li-yaḍrib Zaydun “let Zayd hit” and lā taḍrib Zaydan “do not hit Zayd”.

lessons.title: The seventh kind: nouns that put the muḍāriʿ in jazm
body: The seventh kind brings the first governors that are nouns: nine words that put the muḍāriʿ in jazm “in the meaning of in”: man, mā, matā, mahmā, ayyun, aynamā, annā, ḥaythumā and idhmā. Each carries the meaning of “if” together with a meaning of its own, a person, a thing, a time or a place, and so, like in, it governs two verbs in jazm: the condition and its answer.

They are nouns, not particles, because each stands for something in the sentence. In man yukrimnī ukrimhu, “whoever honours me, I shall honour him”, man is “whoever”, the person who honours; in mā taṣnaʿ aṣnaʿ, “whatever you do, I shall do”, mā is “whatever”, the thing done, the object of taṣnaʿ put before it. In does nothing of the kind: it only links the two verbs.

By their meanings: man is for persons, “whoever”; mā and mahmā for things, “whatever”: mahmā takun akun, “whatever you are, I shall be”; matā and idhmā for time, “whenever”: matā tadhhab adhhab; aynamā, annā and ḥaythumā for place, “wherever”: aynamā tajlis ajlis, “wherever you sit, I shall sit”. Ayyun, “whichever”, takes its meaning from the word it is joined to: ayyahum taḍrib aḍrib, “whichever of them you hit, I shall hit”. Sībawayh held idhmā to be a particle, like in; al-Jurjānī counts it among the nouns.

Look closely at ayyahum. Of the nine, ayyun alone is declinable (muʿrab); the others keep one ending (mabnī). In the book's example it is in naṣb because it is the object of taḍrib, placed before it. So a noun of condition can govern a verb in jazm and be governed by that same verb: ayyahum puts taḍrib in jazm, and taḍrib puts ayyahum in naṣb.

A trap: man and mā are not always nouns of condition. Man jāʾaka? “who came to you?” asks a question, and mā can negate, as in mā Zaydun fāḍilan. The sign of the condition is two verbs, the second an answer to the first, both in jazm.

“whatever”

tasks.prompt: Find the condition and the answer in matā tadhhab adhhab, and give their state and governor.
tasks.answer: Tadhhab is the condition and adhhab the answer; both are in jazm, shown by the sukūn, and matā, a noun of condition meaning “whenever”, governs both.

tasks.prompt: Why is ayyahum in naṣb in ayyahum taḍrib aḍrib?

tasks.prompt: Why are man and mā counted as nouns, while in is a particle?
tasks.answer: Man and mā stand for something in the sentence: the person (“whoever”) or the thing (“whatever”); mā in mā taṣnaʿ is even the object of the verb. In only links the condition to its answer and stands for nothing.

tasks.prompt: Sort the nine by meaning: persons, things, time, place, and the one that takes its meaning from what follows it.
tasks.answer: Persons: man. Things: mā, mahmā. Time: matā, idhmā. Place: aynamā, annā, ḥaythumā. Ayyun takes the meaning of what it is joined to (ayyuhum, “whichever of them”).

text.original: النَّوْعُ السَّابِعُ: أَسْمَاءٌ تَجْزِمُ الْفِعْلَ الْمُضَارِعَ عَلَى مَعْنَى إِنْ، وَهِيَ تِسْعَةُ أَسْمَاءٍ: مَنْ، وَمَا، وَمَتَى، وَمَهْمَا، وَأَيٌّ، وَأَيْنَمَا، وَأَنَّى، وَحَيْثُمَا، وَإِذْمَا.
text.en: The seventh kind: nouns that put the muḍāriʿ in jazm in the meaning of in “if”. They are nine nouns: man, mā, matā, mahmā, ayyun, aynamā, annā, ḥaythumā and idhmā.

text.original: نَحْوُ: مَنْ يُكْرِمْنِي أُكْرِمْهُ، وَمَا تَصْنَعْ أَصْنَعْ، وَمَتَى تَذْهَبْ أَذْهَبْ، وَمَهْمَا تَكُنْ أَكُنْ، وَأَيَّهُمْ تَضْرِبْ أَضْرِبْ، وَأَيْنَمَا تَجْلِسْ أَجْلِسْ، وَأَنَّى تَقْعُدْ أَقْعُدْ، وَحَيْثُمَا تَذْهَبْ أَذْهَبْ، وَإِذْمَا تَفْعَلْ أَفْعَلْ.
text.en: As man yukrimnī ukrimhu “whoever honours me, I shall honour him”, mā taṣnaʿ aṣnaʿ “whatever you do, I shall do”, matā tadhhab adhhab “whenever you go, I shall go”, mahmā takun akun “whatever you are, I shall be”, ayyahum taḍrib aḍrib “whichever of them you hit, I shall hit”, aynamā tajlis ajlis “wherever you sit, I shall sit”, annā taqʿud aqʿud “wherever you sit down, I shall sit down”, ḥaythumā tadhhab adhhab “wherever you go, I shall go” and idhmā tafʿal afʿal “whenever you do [it], I shall do [it]”.

lessons.title: The eighth kind: nouns that put the tamyīz in naṣb
body: The eighth kind is four nouns that “put an indefinite noun in naṣb as a specification (tamyīz)”. A tamyīz removes a vagueness: “eleven” says how many but not of what; rajulan, “men”, says of what. The vague word is the governor; the indefinite noun after it is governed, in naṣb.

The first is ʿashara, “ten”, “when it is compounded with aḥad and ithnān”, that is, in the compound numbers from eleven to nineteen: jāʾanī aḥada ʿashara rajulan, “eleven men came to me”. The book carries the rule on “up to ninety-nine”: from eleven to ninety-nine the counted noun is a single indefinite noun in naṣb. The book itself counts this way on its first two pages: ʿalā thalāthata ʿashara nawʿan, “into thirteen kinds”; sabʿata ʿashara ḥarfan, “seventeen particles”; aḥadun wa-tisʿūna ʿāmilan, “ninety-one governors”.

Compare the numbers outside that range, also in the book's own words. After three to ten and after a hundred the counted noun is in jarr by iḍāfa, not in naṣb: sabʿatu ʿawāmila, “seven governors”, and the title itself, miʾatu ʿāmilin, “a hundred governors”. (ʿAwāmila takes a fatḥa for its jarr, as a diptote.) So miʾa is vague too, but it governs by iḍāfa, not as one of the four nouns of this kind.

Kam, “how many?”, asks a number: kam rajulan ʿindaka, “how many men are with you?”; its tamyīz is a single indefinite noun in naṣb. Kadhā, “so many”, stands for a number not named: kadhā dirhaman ʿindaka, “so many dirhams are with you”. Ka-ayyin, “how many a!”, tells of a great number: ka-ayyin rajulan ʿindaka. Naḥw-i Mīr adds that kam has a second use, telling of a great number, whose tamyīz is in jarr: kam mālin anfaqtu, “how much wealth I have spent!”; only the asking kam belongs here.

A trap: the tamyīz and the ḥāl are both indefinite nouns in naṣb, but they answer different questions. The ḥāl tells the state of someone (“how?”); the tamyīz says what a vague word means (“of what?”). Ask of aḥada ʿashara rajulan, “eleven of what?”: men. That answer is the tamyīz.

tasks.prompt: In kam rajulan ʿindaka, what governs rajulan, and what question does it answer?

tasks.prompt: How do you tell a tamyīz from a ḥāl, since both are indefinite nouns in naṣb?
tasks.answer: The ḥāl tells the state of someone and answers “how?”. The tamyīz removes the vagueness of a word before it and answers “of what?”.

text.original: النَّوْعُ الثَّامِنُ: أَسْمَاءٌ تَنْصِبُ عَلَى التَّمْيِيزِ اسْمًا نَكِرَةً، وَهِيَ أَرْبَعَةُ أَسْمَاءٍ: أَوَّلُهَا عَشَرَةٌ إِذَا رُكِّبَتْ مَعَ أَحَدٍ وَاثْنَيْنِ إِلَى تِسْعَةٍ وَتِسْعِينَ، نَحْوُ: جَاءَنِي أَحَدَ عَشَرَ رَجُلًا، وَثَانِيهَا كَمْ، نَحْوُ: كَمْ رَجُلًا عِنْدَكَ، وَثَالِثُهَا كَذَا، نَحْوُ: كَذَا دِرْهَمًا عِنْدَكَ، وَرَابِعُهَا كَأَيِّنْ، نَحْوُ: كَأَيِّنْ رَجُلًا عِنْدَكَ.
text.en: The eighth kind: nouns that put an indefinite noun in naṣb as a specification (tamyīz). They are four nouns. The first of them is ʿasharatun “ten” when it is compounded with aḥadin and ithnayni, up to ninety-nine, as jāʾanī aḥada ʿashara rajulan “eleven men came to me”; the second is kam, as kam rajulan ʿindaka “how many men are with you?”; the third is kadhā, as kadhā dirhaman ʿindaka “so many dirhams are with you”; and the fourth is ka-ayyin, as ka-ayyin rajulan ʿindaka “how many a man is with you!”.

lessons.title: The ninth kind: the nouns of verbs
body: The ninth kind is “words that are called nouns of verbs” (asmāʾ al-afʿāl): nine words that mean what a verb means and govern as that verb governs, though they take none of a verb's forms: they do not change for past and present or for the persons, and their ending stays the same (they are mabnī). The book calls them “words” (kalimāt), as if to leave them between noun and verb; most grammarians count them nouns, as their name says.

Six put a noun in naṣb, because each means a command whose verb takes an object: ruwayda Zaydan, “give Zayd time”; balha Zaydan, “leave Zayd alone”; dūnaka Zaydan, “take Zayd”; ʿalayka Zaydan, “keep to Zayd”; ḥayyahal Zaydan, “bring Zayd”; hā Zaydan, “take Zayd”. Naḥw-i Mīr explains ruwayda Zaydan as amhilhu, “give him time”: the noun of the verb does what the verb amhil would do.

Dūnaka and ʿalayka are made of a word of place (dūna, “before”) or a preposition (ʿalā, “on”) with the pronoun “you”. The -ka changes with the one addressed, as in the Qurʾān: ʿalaykum anfusakum, “keep to yourselves” (Q 5:105). They are not the preposition ʿalā with its noun: in ʿalayka Zaydan, Zaydan is in naṣb, which no particle of jarr could give.

Three put a noun in rafʿ, because each means a past verb that has a doer and no object: hayhāta Zaydun, “how far away Zayd is!”, which Naḥw-i Mīr explains as baʿuda, “he is far”; shattāna Zaydun wa-ʿAmrun, “how different Zayd and ʿAmr are!”; sarʿāna Zaydun, “how quick Zayd is!”. The noun after them is their doer (fāʿil), in rafʿ. Shattāna needs two nouns, since a difference is always between two.

Birgivī put words like hayhāta under an analogical governor he calls “the meaning of the verb”. Al-Jurjānī lists them by name as heard governors, so the student learns them as a list: each with its meaning and with the state it gives.

terms.en: nouns of verbs: words with a verb's meaning and work
“give time to”: gives naṣb
“keep to”: gives naṣb
“how far!”: gives rafʿ to its doer
“how different!”: gives rafʿ to two

examples.en: ruwayda Zaydan, “give Zayd time”: Zaydan in naṣb
ʿalayka Zaydan, “keep to Zayd”
hayhāta Zaydun, “how far away Zayd is!”: Zaydun its doer, in rafʿ

tasks.prompt: Give the governor and the state of Zayd in dūnaka Zaydan and in sarʿāna Zaydun.
tasks.answer: Dūnaka, a noun of a verb meaning “take”, puts Zaydan in naṣb as its object. Sarʿāna, a noun of a verb meaning “how quick he is!”, puts Zaydun in rafʿ as its doer.

tasks.prompt: Why does shattāna need two nouns?
tasks.answer: It means “how different they are!”, and a difference is between two: Zaydun is its doer and ʿAmrun is joined to him by the wāw, in rafʿ like him.

tasks.prompt: In ʿalayka Zaydan, why is ʿalā not a particle of jarr?
tasks.answer: ʿAlayka here is one word, a noun of a verb meaning “keep to”. Zaydan after it is in naṣb as its object; a particle of jarr would give jarr.

tasks.prompt: Sort the nine into those that give naṣb and those that give rafʿ, and say why each group governs as it does.
tasks.answer: Naṣb: ruwayda, balha, dūnaka, ʿalayka, ḥayyahal, hā; they mean commands whose verbs take an object. Rafʿ: hayhāta, shattāna, sarʿāna; they mean past verbs with a doer and no object.

text.original: النَّوْعُ التَّاسِعُ: كَلِمَاتٌ تُسَمَّى أَسْمَاءَ الْأَفْعَالِ، بَعْضُهَا تَرْفَعُ وَبَعْضُهَا تَنْصِبُ، وَهِيَ تِسْعُ كَلِمَاتٍ. النَّاصِبُ مِنْهَا سِتُّ كَلِمَاتٍ: رُوَيْدَ، وَبَلْهَ، وَدُونَكَ، وَعَلَيْكَ، وَحَيَّهَلْ، وَهَا، نَحْوُ: رُوَيْدَ زَيْدًا، وَبَلْهَ زَيْدًا، وَدُونَكَ زَيْدًا، وَعَلَيْكَ زَيْدًا، وَحَيَّهَلْ زَيْدًا، وَهَا زَيْدًا.
text.en: The ninth kind: words that are called nouns of verbs (asmāʾ al-afʿāl); some of them put in rafʿ and some in naṣb. They are nine words. Those of them that put in naṣb are six words: ruwayda, balha, dūnaka, ʿalayka, ḥayyahal and hā, as ruwayda Zaydan “give Zayd time”, balha Zaydan “leave Zayd alone”, dūnaka Zaydan “take Zayd”, ʿalayka Zaydan “keep to Zayd”, ḥayyahal Zaydan “bring Zayd” and hā Zaydan “take Zayd”.

text.original: وَالرَّافِعُ مِنْهَا ثَلَاثُ كَلِمَاتٍ: هَيْهَاتَ، وَشَتَّانَ، وَسَرْعَانَ، نَحْوُ: هَيْهَاتَ زَيْدٌ، وَشَتَّانَ زَيْدٌ وَعَمْرٌو، وَسَرْعَانَ زَيْدٌ.
text.en: Those of them that put in rafʿ are three words: hayhāta, shattāna and sarʿāna, as hayhāta Zaydun “how far away Zayd is!”, shattāna Zaydun wa-ʿAmrun “how different Zayd and ʿAmr are!” and sarʿāna Zaydun “how quick Zayd is!”.

lessons.title: The tenth kind: kāna and its sisters
body: The tenth kind brings the governors that are verbs: thirteen “incomplete verbs” (afʿāl nāqiṣa) that “put the noun in rafʿ and the predicate in naṣb”. Like inna, they come before a sentence of subject and predicate; unlike inna, they leave the subject in rafʿ and put the predicate in naṣb: Zaydun qāʾimun becomes kāna Zaydun qāʾiman, “Zayd was standing”. The first is called the noun (ism) of kāna, the second its predicate (khabar).

They are called incomplete because a noun in rafʿ does not complete them: kāna Zaydun, “Zayd was”, leaves the hearer waiting for “was what?”. A complete verb says its sense with its doer alone, as qāma Zaydun, “Zayd stood up”.

Their meanings: kāna, “was”, puts the predicate in the past; ṣāra, “became”, turns one state into another: ṣāra al-faqīru ghaniyyan, “the poor man became rich”. Aṣbaḥa, amsā and aḍḥā tie the predicate to the morning, the evening and the forenoon; ẓalla to the whole day: ẓalla Zaydun ṣāʾiman, “Zayd stayed fasting all day”; bāta to the night: bāta Zaydun nāʾiman. Laysa, “is not”, negates. The four with mā, mā bariḥa, mā fatiʾa, mā zāla and mā infakka, mean “did not cease”, that is, “still”: mā zāla Zaydun ʿāliman, “Zayd is still learned”. To deny ceasing is to say that a thing lasts.

Mā dāma, “as long as”, is different: its mā is not a negation but makes the verb a span of time: ijlis mā dāma Zaydun jālisan, “sit as long as Zayd is sitting”, that is, for the time of his sitting. So mā dāma does not begin a sentence; it hangs on a sentence before it, here ijlis, “sit!”.

Two traps. In the four verbs of continuance the mā is part of the governor: without the negation they do not work in this way. And several of these verbs can also be complete, with a doer and no predicate, when they mean “to be, to happen”: wa-in kāna dhū ʿusratin, “and if there is someone in hardship” (Q 2:280). Kāna there has only its doer, dhū ʿusratin.

terms.en: the incomplete verbs: kāna and its sisters
the noun of kāna (in rafʿ) and its predicate (in naṣb)

text.en: The tenth kind: incomplete verbs (afʿāl nāqiṣa) that put the noun in rafʿ and the predicate in naṣb. They are thirteen verbs: kāna, ṣāra, aṣbaḥa, amsā, aḍḥā, ẓalla, bāta, mā bariḥa, mā fatiʾa, mā zāla, mā infakka, mā dāma and laysa.

text.original: نَحْوُ: كَانَ زَيْدٌ قَائِمًا، وَصَارَ الْفَقِيرُ غَنِيًّا، وَأَصْبَحَ زَيْدٌ عَالِمًا، وَأَمْسَى زَيْدٌ قَارِئًا، وَأَضْحَى زَيْدٌ مُسَافِرًا، وَظَلَّ زَيْدٌ صَائِمًا، وَبَاتَ زَيْدٌ نَائِمًا، وَمَا بَرِحَ زَيْدٌ عَالِمًا، وَمَا فَتِئَ زَيْدٌ قَائِمًا، وَمَا زَالَ زَيْدٌ عَالِمًا، وَمَا انْفَكَّ بَكْرٌ عَاقِلًا، وَاجْلِسْ مَا دَامَ زَيْدٌ جَالِسًا، وَلَيْسَ زَيْدٌ قَائِمًا.
text.en: As kāna Zaydun qāʾiman “Zayd was standing”, ṣāra al-faqīru ghaniyyan “the poor man became rich”, aṣbaḥa Zaydun ʿāliman “Zayd was learned in the morning”, amsā Zaydun qāriʾan “Zayd was reading in the evening”, aḍḥā Zaydun musāfiran “Zayd was travelling in the forenoon”, ẓalla Zaydun ṣāʾiman “Zayd stayed fasting all day”, bāta Zaydun nāʾiman “Zayd spent the night asleep”, mā bariḥa Zaydun ʿāliman “Zayd has not ceased to be learned”, mā fatiʾa Zaydun qāʾiman “Zayd has not ceased standing”, mā zāla Zaydun ʿāliman “Zayd is still learned”, mā infakka Bakrun ʿāqilan “Bakr has not ceased to be sensible”, ijlis mā dāma Zaydun jālisan “sit as long as Zayd is sitting” and laysa Zaydun qāʾiman “Zayd is not standing”.

lessons.title: The eleventh kind: the verbs of approach
body: The eleventh kind is four verbs “of approach” (al-muqāraba) that “put one noun in rafʿ”: ʿasā, kāda, karaba and awshaka. They say that the action of another verb is near: ʿasā Zaydun an yakhruja, “perhaps Zayd will go out”; kāda Zaydun an yakhruja, “Zayd was about to go out”; karaba Zaydun yakhruju, “Zayd was near to going out”; awshaka Zaydun yajīʾu, “Zayd was on the point of coming”. ʿAsā is the verb of hope (rajāʾ): it hopes that the act will come; the other three say that it was close.

After the noun comes a muḍāriʿ, the action that is near, and as a rule not a single noun as after kāna: the book says kāda Zaydun an yakhruja, not “kāda Zaydun khārijan”. The muḍāriʿ may come with an or without it, and the book's examples show both.

“One noun”: al-Jurjānī names only the noun they put in rafʿ, the one whose action is near. Most grammarians count them with kāna, as Naḥw-i Mīr does: Zayd is their noun, in rafʿ, and the verb after it is their predicate, standing in the place of a word in naṣb (fī maḥall naṣb). Naḥw-i Mīr adds a second way with ʿasā: ʿasā an yakhruja Zaydun, where an yakhruja is the doer of ʿasā and no predicate is needed.

On an, later books give the usual practice: with ʿasā and awshaka the muḍāriʿ mostly takes an, with kāda and karaba mostly not; so kāda Zaydun yakhruju is the commoner form, as in the Qurʾān: yakādu zaytuhā yuḍīʾu, “its oil would almost give light” (Q 24:35). The book's kāda Zaydun an yakhruja and awshaka Zaydun yajīʾu are the less common uses; both are allowed.
A trap: ʿasā is a verb, though it does not change for present or command; it is used only in this past form. Kāda changes like other verbs: the Qurʾān says yakādu.

lessons.title: The twelfth kind: the verbs of praise and blame
body: The twelfth kind is four verbs of praise and blame, niʿma, biʾsa, sāʾa and ḥabbadhā, which “put in rafʿ the generic noun made definite by the lām”: niʿma al-rajulu Zaydun, “what an excellent man Zayd is!”; biʾsa al-rajulu ʿAmrun, “what a bad man ʿAmr is!”; sāʾa al-rajulu Bakrun, “what an evil man Bakr is!”; ḥabbadhā al-rajulu Zaydun, “how lovable a man Zayd is!”. Niʿma and ḥabbadhā praise; biʾsa and sāʾa blame.

The sentence has three parts. The verb, niʿma; its doer, al-rajulu, a generic noun (ism jins) with al-, “the man” in the sense of man as a kind; and the one singled out for the praise, Zaydun, called al-makhṣūṣ bi-l-madḥ (or bi-l-dhamm). The verb praises the kind, and the last noun names the one meant.

The book names only the doer, which the verb governs. Zaydun is in rafʿ too, and the commentators give two readings of it: it is a subject (mubtadaʾ) whose predicate is the sentence before it, niʿma al-rajulu; or it is the predicate of a subject left out, “he is Zayd”.

These verbs do not change: niʿma and biʾsa have no muḍāriʿ and no command, and they keep their meaning of praise and blame only in this form. Ḥabbadhā is two words joined: the verb ḥabba, “to be dear”, and dhā, “this”; Ibn Mālik names dhā as its doer (al-fāʿilu dhā). The book counts it with niʿma because it praises in the same way.

A trap: Zaydun is not the doer of niʿma, though it is the noun the sentence is about. The doer is al-rajulu; Zaydun is the one singled out. And sāʾa here is not the sāʾa of everyday speech, “it grieved”, with its full conjugation; in this use it works like biʾsa.

They are four verbs: niʿma, biʾsa, sāʾa and ḥabbadhā, as niʿma al-rajulu Zaydun “what an excellent man Zayd is!”, biʾsa al-rajulu ʿAmrun “what a bad man ʿAmr is!”, sāʾa al-rajulu Bakrun “what an evil man Bakr is!” and ḥabbadhā al-rajulu Zaydun “how lovable a man Zayd is!”.

lessons.title: The thirteenth kind: the verbs of doubt and certainty
body: The last heard kind is seven verbs “of doubt and certainty” that “come before two nouns, the second of which refers to the first, and put both in naṣb”: ḥasibtu, ẓanantu, khiltu, raʾaytu, ʿalimtu, wajadtu and zaʿamtu. The two nouns were a subject and its predicate: Zaydun fāḍilun, “Zayd is excellent”, becomes ḥasibtu Zaydan fāḍilan, “I reckoned Zayd excellent”. “The second refers to the first” means that the second says something of the same person: the excellent one is Zayd.

The book gives them in the first person, ḥasibtu “I reckoned”, ẓanantu “I thought”, because this is how they are used: the speaker reports his own judgment. The commentators divide them by the strength of that judgment: ḥasibtu, ẓanantu, khiltu and zaʿamtu for doubt or opinion; raʾaytu, ʿalimtu and wajadtu for certainty. Later books call all of them “verbs of the heart” (afʿāl al-qulūb), since they name what happens in the mind.

Read the examples with that in mind. Ẓanantu Bakran nāʾiman, “I thought Bakr asleep”, is an opinion; ʿalimtu Zaydan amīnan, “I knew Zayd to be trustworthy”, is knowledge. Zaʿamtu, “I claimed”, is said of a judgment that may well be false, and the book's example fits it: zaʿamtu al-shayṭāna shakūran, “I claimed Satan to be grateful”. The grammarians call the first noun the first object (al-mafʿūl al-awwal) and the second the second object (al-mafʿūl al-thānī).

Raʾaytu here is not seeing with the eye: raʾaytu Zaydan ʿāqilan is “I saw Zayd to be sensible”, a judgment of the mind, with two objects. Seeing with the eye takes one object, as in the first kind: raʾaytu al-qawma, “I saw the people”. Wajadtu too means “I found him to be”: wajadtu al-bayta rahīnan, “I found the house pledged”.

A trap: the second noun in naṣb looks like a ḥāl, a word of state, but it cannot be left out. Ẓanantu Zaydan alone does not say what I thought of Zayd; the sentence needs fāḍilan or nāʾiman to be complete. That is why both nouns are objects of the verb.

text.original: النَّوْعُ الثَّالِثَ عَشَرَ: أَفْعَالُ الشَّكِّ وَالْيَقِينِ، تَدْخُلُ عَلَى اسْمَيْنِ ثَانِيهِمَا عِبَارَةٌ عَنِ الْأَوَّلِ، تَنْصِبُهُمَا، وَهِيَ سَبْعَةُ أَفْعَالٍ: حَسِبْتُ، وَظَنَنْتُ، وَخِلْتُ، وَرَأَيْتُ، وَعَلِمْتُ، وَوَجَدْتُ، وَزَعَمْتُ.
text.en: The thirteenth kind: the verbs of doubt and certainty (afʿāl al-shakk wa-al-yaqīn), which come before two nouns, the second of which refers to the first, and put both in naṣb. They are seven verbs: ḥasibtu “I reckoned”, ẓanantu “I thought”, khiltu “I imagined”, raʾaytu “I saw”, ʿalimtu “I knew”, wajadtu “I found” and zaʿamtu “I claimed”.

text.original: نَحْوُ: حَسِبْتُ زَيْدًا فَاضِلًا، وَظَنَنْتُ بَكْرًا نَائِمًا، وَخِلْتُ خَالِدًا قَائِمًا، وَرَأَيْتُ زَيْدًا عَاقِلًا، وَعَلِمْتُ زَيْدًا أَمِينًا، وَوَجَدْتُ الْبَيْتَ رَهِينًا، وَزَعَمْتُ الشَّيْطَانَ شَكُورًا.
text.en: As ḥasibtu Zaydan fāḍilan “I reckoned Zayd excellent”, ẓanantu Bakran nāʾiman “I thought Bakr asleep”, khiltu Khālidan qāʾiman “I imagined Khālid standing”, raʾaytu Zaydan ʿāqilan “I saw Zayd to be sensible”, ʿalimtu Zaydan amīnan “I knew Zayd to be trustworthy”, wajadtu al-bayta rahīnan “I found the house pledged” and zaʿamtu al-shayṭāna shakūran “I claimed Satan to be grateful”.

parts.title: The analogical and the abstract governors

lessons.title: The seven analogical governors
body: After the ninety-one heard governors come seven analogical ones (qiyāsiyya). They are not single words but classes of word: whatever word belongs to the class governs by rule, without being listed. So “the verb in general” (al-fiʿl ʿalā al-iṭlāq) is one governor, though it covers countless verbs: every verb governs its doer, and a transitive verb its object as well.

The verb gives rafʿ to its doer and, if it is transitive, naṣb to its object: ḍaraba Zaydun ʿAmran, “Zayd hit ʿAmr”. Four more are nouns made from verbs that work as their verbs work. Naḥw-i Mīr, read before this book, gives an example of each: the active participle, Zaydun ḍāribun abūhu ʿAmran, “Zayd, his father is hitting ʿAmr”, where ḍārib does what ḍaraba does; the passive participle, Zaydun maḍrūbun abūhu, “Zayd, his father is beaten”; the resembling adjective (al-ṣifa al-mushabbaha), an adjective of a lasting quality, Zaydun ḥasanun ghulāmuhu, “Zayd, his servant is handsome”; and the maṣdar, aʿjabanī ḍarbu Zaydin ʿAmran, “Zayd's hitting ʿAmr pleased me”.

The last two concern nouns. “The noun annexed to another noun”, the muḍāf, puts the second in jarr: yā ʿAbda Allāhi, yawmi al-jumuʿati, and the title miʾatu ʿāmilin. “Every noun that is complete and has no need of annexation” puts its tamyīz in naṣb: a noun is complete when it ends in tanwīn or in a nūn and so cannot be joined to what follows, as tisʿūna in aḥadun wa-tisʿūna ʿāmilan. The eighth kind gave four such nouns by name; here the rule covers them all.

This is what an analogical governor gives: once you know that the active participle works like its verb, every active participle of every verb is a governor. That is why there are only seven, and why they are learnt as rules, not as lists. Later books, Naḥw-i Mīr among them, add the conditions under which each works: the active participle, for one, works when it means the present or the future and leans on a word before it, such as a subject (Zaydun ḍāribun…).

A trap: do not count a verb's work twice. In ḍaraba Zaydun ʿAmran there is one governor, ḍaraba, for both Zaydun and ʿAmran. And a muḍāf may itself be governed: in yā ʿAbda Allāhi, ʿAbda is governed by yā and governs Allāhi.

tasks.arabic: ضَرَبَ زَيْدٌ عَمْرًا — زَيْدٌ حَسَنٌ غُلَامُهُ — يَوْمِ الْجُمُعَةِ — تِسْعُونَ عَامِلًا
tasks.answer: ʿAmran: the verb ḍaraba (naṣb, its object). Ghulāmuhu: the resembling adjective ḥasanun (rafʿ). Al-jumuʿati: the muḍāf yawmi (jarr). ʿĀmilan: the complete noun tisʿūna (naṣb, as tamyīz).

tasks.prompt: In aʿjabanī ḍarbu Zaydin ʿAmran, what does the maṣdar ḍarb govern, and how does it show that it works like its verb?
tasks.answer: Ḍarbu is joined to Zaydin, the hitter, who is in jarr by the iḍāfa, and it puts ʿAmran, the one hit, in naṣb as its object, as the verb ḍaraba would.

tasks.prompt: Why are there only seven analogical governors, when the heard ones are ninety-one?
tasks.answer: Each analogical governor is a class with a rule (every verb, every active participle…), so one rule covers countless words. The heard governors have no rule and must be counted one by one.

text.original: وَالْقِيَاسِيَّةُ مِنْهَا سَبْعَةُ عَوَامِلَ: الْفِعْلُ عَلَى الْإِطْلَاقِ، وَالصِّفَةُ الْمُشَبَّهَةُ، وَاسْمُ الْفَاعِلِ، وَاسْمُ الْمَفْعُولِ، وَالْمَصْدَرُ، وَالِاسْمُ الَّذِي أُضِيفَ إِلَى اسْمٍ آخَرَ، وَكُلُّ اسْمٍ تَمَّ وَاسْتَغْنَى عَنِ الْإِضَافَةِ.
text.en: And the analogical ones are seven governors: the verb in general; the resembling adjective (al-ṣifa al-mushabbaha); the active participle; the passive participle; the maṣdar; the noun that is annexed to another noun; and every noun that is complete and has no need of annexation.

lessons.title: The two abstract governors
body: The book closes with two governors that are not words at all: “they have no governor visible in the wording”. Every ending has a cause; when no word stands before a noun or a verb to cause it, the grammarians name a cause in the meaning, an abstract (maʿnawī) governor.

The first governs the subject and the predicate: “the beginning” (al-ibtidāʾ), a noun's being put at the head of a sentence, free of any expressed governor, so that something may be said of it. In Zaydun fī al-dāri, “Zayd is in the house”, no word comes before Zaydun; the ibtidāʾ puts it in rafʿ. The book makes the ibtidāʾ the governor of the subject and the predicate together. This is one view among several: Ibn Mālik follows another, that the subject is put in rafʿ by the ibtidāʾ and the predicate by the subject.

The second governs the muḍāriʿ in rafʿ: “its standing in the place of the noun” (wuqūʿuhu bi-mawqiʿi al-ism). Yaḍribu in Zaydun yaḍribu, “Zayd hits”, stands where a noun could stand, as in Zaydun ḍāribun, and that is what puts it in rafʿ. This is the view of the Baṣran grammarians. Al-Farrāʾ and other Kūfans say that the muḍāriʿ is in rafʿ because it is free of any governor of naṣb or jazm; Ibn Mālik follows them in his Alfiyya.

With these two the system is closed. Every ending now has a cause: one of the ninety-one heard governors, one of the seven analogical ones, or one of these two. A student parsing Zaydun fī al-dāri says that Zaydun is a subject, in rafʿ by the ibtidāʾ; parsing Zaydun yaḍribu, he says that yaḍribu is in rafʿ because it stands in the place of a noun. When lam comes, lam yaḍrib Zaydun, an expressed governor has entered, and the abstract one gives way.

The book ends with tammat, “it is finished”: a hundred governors in a few pages. The next naḥw book of the Indian path, Hidāyat al-naḥw, takes the same matter in the order of the noun, the verb and the particle, with definitions and reasons.

tasks.prompt: Name the governor of each word in Zaydun fī al-dāri, as this book counts them.
tasks.answer: Zaydun: the ibtidāʾ, an abstract governor (rafʿ). Al-dāri: fī, a particle of jarr of the first kind (jarr). The predicate, fī al-dāri, is also governed by the ibtidāʾ in the book's view.

tasks.prompt: Why is yaḍribu in rafʿ in Zaydun yaḍribu, and why is it not in rafʿ in lam yaḍrib Zaydun?
tasks.answer: In Zaydun yaḍribu no word governs it; it stands where a noun could stand (Zaydun ḍāribun), and that abstract governor puts it in rafʿ. In lam yaḍrib Zaydun the particle lam, an expressed governor, has entered and put it in jazm.

tasks.prompt: Give the Baṣran view and the Kūfan view of what puts the muḍāriʿ in rafʿ.
tasks.answer: Baṣran, the view of this book: its standing in the place of a noun. Kūfan (al-Farrāʾ), followed by Ibn Mālik: its being free of any governor of naṣb or jazm.

tasks.prompt: Sum up the hundred governors of the book by their divisions.
tasks.answer: Ninety-eight expressed and two abstract. The expressed: ninety-one heard, in thirteen kinds (six of particles, three of nouns, four of verbs), and seven analogical. The abstract: the ibtidāʾ, and the muḍāriʿ's standing in the place of a noun.

text.original: وَالْمَعْنَوِيَّةُ مِنْهَا عَدَدَانِ: الْعَامِلُ فِي الْمُبْتَدَإِ وَالْخَبَرِ، وَهُوَ الِابْتِدَاءُ، وَالْعَامِلُ فِي الْفِعْلِ الْمُضَارِعِ، وَهُوَ وُقُوعُهُ بِمَوْقِعِ الِاسْمِ، وَلَيْسَ لَهَا عَامِلٌ ظَاهِرٌ فِي اللَّفْظِ. تَمَّتْ.
text.en: And the abstract ones are two in number: the governor of the subject and the predicate (al-mubtadaʾ wa-al-khabar), which is the beginning (al-ibtidāʾ); and the governor of the muḍāriʿ, which is its standing in the place of the noun. They have no governor visible in the wording. Finished.
